newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala telephone law faces legal battle.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala telephone law faces legal battle.

text.p: A court challenge presented by unions against Guatemala's new telecommunications law could hold up the opening up of the telephone market for at least three months, officials said on Tuesday.

"We don't think the process will be held up more than three months. But if the law is slowed down (more than that) we will open up the market by (executive) order," Alfredo Guzman, general manager of the Guatemalan Telecommunications Company (Guatel), told a news conference.

Congress passed a new telecommunications law in October, opening up the state-owned industry to international competition for both local and long-distance telephone service. Later, Guatel itself will become a private company.

Two telecommunications unions presented a legal challenge to the new law on Monday, asking the Constitutional Court to suspend the law, while considering whether certain parts of it are unconstitutional.
The court, the highest judicial authority in the country, has not yet ruled on whether to suspend the law.
The suit by the unions questioned a variety of technical aspects of the law.
Many union workers worry that as the Guatemalan telecommunications industry becomes more competitive, inefficient Guatel will lay off excess employees, who will not find work with the new companies.
Guzmn called the lawsuit a "political maneuver."
He said, "It's a good law that will allow a large quantity of investment in the country to install telephones where there are none."
Guatel does not have the capital to invest in improving service.

Guatemala has four telephone lines for every 100 people. A million requests for lines are backlogged at Guatel. In Guatemala City alone, 425,000 requests for lines are waiting to be filled. More than 100,000 lines have been paid for, some up to 18 months ago, and have not been installed.
